issues.title: varlen_attn cuDNN backend: backward is not deterministic and ignores torch.use_deterministic_algorithms
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

 The cuDNN backend of `torch.nn.attention.varlen.varlen_attn` produces a different `dq` on every backward run, even with `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)`. It neither raises nor warns, so a run in deterministic mode. So a run in deterministic mode with cuDNN backend silently loses the reproducibility.

### Versions

### Versions

  torch 2.16.0.dev20261030+cu132, CUDA 13.2, cuDNN 9.26 (92600), NVIDIA H100.

### Repro (H100):

  ```python
  import torch
  from torch.nn.attention import SDPBackend, sdpa_kernel
  from torch.nn.attention.varlen import varlen_attn

  torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)
  torch.manual_seed(0)

  seq_lens = [1024, 3072, 2048, 2048]  # 4 packed documents
  cu_seq = torch.tensor([0] + seq_lens, device="cuda").cumsum(0).to(torch.int32)
  total, max_len = sum(seq_lens), max(seq_lens)
  q, k, v = (
      torch.randn(total, 16, 128, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
      for _ in range(3)
  )
  grad_out = torch.randn_like(q)


  def dq(backend):
      q_ = q.detach().requires_grad_()
      with sdpa_kernel([backend]):
          varlen_attn(q_, k, v, cu_seq, cu_seq, max_len, max_len).backward(grad_out)
      return q_.grad


  for backend in (SDPBackend.CUDNN_ATTENTION, SDPBackend.FLASH_ATTENTION):
      ref = dq(backend)
      num_diff = sum(not torch.equal(ref, dq(backend)) for _ in range(20))
      print(f"{backend.name}: {num_diff} of 20 runs have a different dq")
  ```

  Output:

  ```
  CUDNN_ATTENTION: 20 of 20 runs have a different dq
  FLASH_ATTENTION: 0 of 20 runs have a different dq

issues.title: Deterministic scan: replace PyTorch's custom kernel with CCCL
issues.body:
## Background PyTorch's [deterministic cumulative sum](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/aten/src/ATen/cuda/cub.cuh#L457) (used when `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` is set) runs a custom CUDA kernel in two passes: the first pass adds up each block, the second pass reads the input again and scans each block starting from the sum of the blocks before it. Doing it this way keeps the add order fixed, so the result is the same every run, but it reads the input twice. Scan speed is limited by memory, so that extra read means this approach can only reach about 66% (2 of 3 memory passes) of the speed a single-pass scan can hit. CCCL now makes `cub::DeviceScan` reproducible on its own through a `run_to_run` env knob ([CCCL PR #9098](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cccl/pull/9098)), will be available in the upcoming CCCL 3.5 release. (Check here for the related blogpost [Controlling Floating Point Determinism in NVIDIA CCCL](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/controlling-floating-point-determinism-in-nvidia-cccl/), and [docs] (https://nvidia.github.io/cccl/unstable/cccl/determinism.html)). Building against the latest CCCL, instead of the copy that ships with the CUDA toolkit, lets us delete the custom kernel and call `DeviceScan` instead. ## Build change: fetch CCCL from GitHub Today PyTorch uses CCCL from the headers bundled inside the CUDA toolkit (CTK). The `run_to_run` deterministic scan arrives in CCCL 3.5 (upcoming release), which is newer than the CCCL any released CTK ships with, so adopting it means building PyTorch against CCCL 3.5 instead of the toolkit's copy. There are a few ways to make this possible, one we tried locally is to do CMake fetch that pulls latest CCCL (master) from GitHub and prepends it to the include path, ahead of the toolkit's copy. This is safe because of CCCL's [compatibility policy](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cccl#cuda-toolkit-ctk-compatibility): the latest CCCL stays backward compatible with the current and previous CTK major versions (two major versions), and CCCL can be upgraded on its own, independently of the toolkit. So PyTorch keeps building against the CUDA version it already uses, with only the CCCL headers moved forward. ## Determinism usage The whole deterministic path becomes a single `DeviceScan` call with a `run_to_run` env: ```cpp auto env = ::cuda::std::execution::env{ stream, ::cuda::execution::require(::cuda::execution::determinism::run_to_run), caching_allocator_resource{}}; cub::DeviceScan::InclusiveSum(input, output, num_items, env); ``` ## Lines of code (`cub.cuh`, scan only) | | Lines | |---|---| | Removed (custom two-pass kernel + helpers) | - 126 | | Added (CCCL `DeviceScan` path) | + 21 | | **Net** | **-105** | ## Performance PyTorch's two-pass kernel at best reaches a peak of 32%, while the new CCCL's `cub::DeviceScan` reaches about 91% on large inputs, because it reads the input once instead of twice, also because of the latest warp specialized kernel (warpspeed-lookahead-scan).
NVIDIA B200 - cumsum, fp32 (Ref = current PyTorch, Cmp = CCCL) | Elements | Ref Time | Ref Noise | Cmp Time | Cmp Noise | Diff | %Diff | Status | |------------|------------|-------------|------------|-------------|--------------|---------|----------| | 2^16 | 20.942 us | 7.12% | 23.195 us | 12.79% | 2.253 us | 10.76% | 🔴 SLOW | | 2^18 | 21.356 us | 3.12% | 23.387 us | 53.42% | 2.031 us | 9.51% | 🔴 SLOW | | 2^20 | 22.739 us | 5.02% | 25.528 us | 5.56% | 2.789 us | 12.26% | 🔴 SLOW | | 2^22 | 33.401 us | 5.80% | 31.403 us | 5.37% | -1.998 us | -5.98% | 🟢 FAST | | 2^24 | 78.007 us | 1.27% | 48.413 us | 38.83% | -29.594 us | -37.94% | 🟢 FAST | | 2^26 | 249.637 us | 0.90% | 104.738 us | 2.13% | -144.898 us | -58.04% | 🟢 FAST | | 2^28 | 904.171 us | 0.71% | 336.952 us | 0.52% | -567.219 us | -62.73% | 🟢 FAST | | 2^30 | 3.508 ms | 0.24% | 1.254 ms | 0.50% | -2254.109 us | -64.26% | 🟢 FAST | | 2^32 | 13.888 ms | 0.10% | 4.922 ms | 0.08% | -8965.687 us | -64.56% | 🟢 FAST |
On large inputs CCCL is up to **2.8x faster** (2^32: 13.9 ms -> 4.9 ms), starting from about 1.6x at 2^24 and staying near 2.8x for the biggest sizes. ## Takeaway Building against the latest CCCL, instead of the version bundled with the CUDA toolkit (CTK), is what makes this work and it is seamless. We remove 105 lines of hand-written scan code and get a faster, reproducible `DeviceScan` in return. As CCCL adds more features, staying on the latest version lets PyTorch use them right away instead of waiting for a toolkit release. cc @ptrblck @msaroufim @eqy @tinglvv @nWEIdia @mruberry @kurtamohler

issues.title: torch.compile() produces inconsistent outputs with models containing dropout and in-place ReLU operations
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Description: When compiling models using torch.compile(), we observe numerical discrepancies in forward pass outputs due to non-deterministic operation reordering (particularly with nn.Dropout and nn.ReLU(inplace=True)). These differences exceed floating-point tolerance thresholds (max diff ≈ 2.9e-3), causing torch.allclose(atol=1e-5) to fail despite identical training configurations.
﻿
code:
'''
import os
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import torch.optim as optim
from torchvision import datasets, transforms
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader


class ShallowCNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_classes=10):
        super().__init__()

        self.features = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(3, 32, kernel_size=3, padding=1), 
            nn.BatchNorm2d(32),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.MaxPool2d(2),  # [B,32,16,16]

            nn.Conv2d(32, 64, kernel_size=3, padding=1), 
            nn.BatchNorm2d(64),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.MaxPool2d(2)  # [B,64,8,8]
        )

        self.classifier = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Flatten(),
            nn.Linear(64 * 8 * 8, 128),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Dropout(0.5),
            nn.Linear(128, num_classes)
        )

        self._init_weights()

    def _init_weights(self):
        for m in self.modules():
            if isinstance(m, nn.Conv2d):
                nn.init.kaiming_normal_(m.weight, mode='fan_out', nonlinearity='relu')
                if m.bias is not None:
                    nn.init.constant_(m.bias, 0)
            elif isinstance(m, nn.Linear):
                nn.init.normal_(m.weight, 0, 0.01)
                nn.init.constant_(m.bias, 0)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.features(x)
        return self.classifier(x)
def train(model, device, train_loader, optimizer, epoch):
    model.train()
    for batch_idx, (data, target) in enumerate(train_loader):
        data, target = data.to(device), target.to(device)
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        output = model(data)
        loss = F.cross_entropy(output, target)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        if batch_idx % 100 == 0:
            print(f'Epoch {epoch}, Batch {batch_idx}, Loss: {loss.item():.4f}')
def test(model, device, test_loader):
    model.eval()
    correct = 0
    with torch.no_grad():
        for data, target in test_loader:
            data, target = data.to(device), target.to(device)
            output = model(data)
            pred = output.argmax(dim=1, keepdim=True)
            correct += pred.eq(target.view_as(pred)).sum().item()
    acc = 100. * correct / len(test_loader.dataset)
    print(f'Test Accuracy: {acc:.2f}%')
    return acc
if __name__ == "__main__":
    torch.manual_seed(42)
    torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(42)
    torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True

    device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
    batch_size = 128
    epochs = 1
    lr = 0.01

    transform = transforms.Compose([
        transforms.RandomHorizontalFlip(),
        transforms.RandomCrop(32, padding=4),
        transforms.ToTensor(),
        transforms.Normalize((0.4914, 0.4822, 0.4465), (0.2023, 0.1994, 0.2010))
    ])

    train_set = datasets.CIFAR10('./data', train=True, download=True, transform=transform)
    test_set = datasets.CIFAR10('./data', train=False, transform=transform)

    train_loader = DataLoader(train_set, batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=True)
    test_loader = DataLoader(test_set, batch_size=batch_size)

    model = ShallowCNN().to(device)
    optimizer = optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=lr, momentum=0.9, weight_decay=5e-4)

    best_acc = 0
    for epoch in range(1, epochs + 1):
        train(model, device, train_loader, optimizer, epoch)
        acc = test(model, device, test_loader)
        if acc > best_acc:
            best_acc = acc
            torch.save(model.state_dict(), 'shallow_cnn_best.pth')

    print(f"\nBest Accuracy: {best_acc:.2f}%")
    print(f"Total Parameters: {sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) / 1e6:.2f}M")

    model.eval()  
    test_data, _ = next(iter(test_loader))
    test_data = test_data.to(device)

    with torch.no_grad():
        output_original = model(test_data)
        compiled_model = torch.compile(model)
        output_compiled = compiled_model(test_data)
        # Print differences directly
        print("\n" + "=" * 50)
        print("Output differences between original and compiled models")
        print("Class-wise differences for first 3 samples:")
        for i in range(3):  # Only show first 3 samples
            diff = (output_original - output_compiled)[i]
            print(f"\nSample {i} class differences:")
            for j, val in enumerate(diff):
                print(f"Class {j}: {val.item():.6e}", end=" | ")
                if (j + 1) % 5 == 0:  # Show 5 classes per line
                    print()
        print("\n" + "=" * 50)
        max_diff = torch.max(torch.abs(output_original - output_compiled)).item()
        mean_diff = torch.mean(torch.abs(output_original - output_compiled)).item()

    print("Original model contains NaN:", torch.isnan(output_original).any())
    print("Compiled model contains INF:", torch.isinf(output_compiled).any())
    print("\n" + "=" * 50)
    print("Compilation comparison results")
    print(f"Maximum absolute difference: {max_diff:.6e}")
    print(f"Mean absolute difference: {mean_diff:.6e}")
    print(f"Are outputs consistent (1e-5 tolerance): {torch.allclose(output_original, output_compiled, atol=1e-5)}")
    print("=" * 50 + "\n")
 
'''
